<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
In ZFC there is a set-sized, countably infinite orthomodular lattice $L$,
generated by three specified elements, with no embedding into any
set-sized $\sigma$-complete orthomodular lattice. Consequently, $L$ has
no embedding into any set-sized complete orthomodular lattice.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:dual}
In any OML,
\begin{align}
 z\le b&\ \Longrightarrow\ b\wedge(b'\vee z)=z,\label{eq:dual}\\
 b'\vee x&=b'\vee\pi_b(x).\label{eq:E}
\end{align}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
If $z\le b$, apply~\eqref{eq:om} to $b'\le z'$ to obtain
$z'=b'\vee(z'\wedge b)$. Taking complements gives~\eqref{eq:dual}.
Applying~\eqref{eq:om} to $b'\le b'\vee x$ gives
$b'\vee x=b'\vee((b'\vee x)\wedge b)=b'\vee\pi_b(x)$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:adjunction}
For arbitrary $b,x,y$ in an OML,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:adjunction}
       \pi_b(x)\le y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
       x\le b'\vee(b\wedge y).
\end{equation}
If $Y$ has an actual supremum $j$, then $\pi_b[Y]$ has a supremum and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sup}
                       \pi_b(j)=\bigvee_{y\in Y}\pi_b(y).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
If $\pi_b(x)\le y$, then $\pi_b(x)\le b\wedge y$.
Equation~\eqref{eq:E} gives
$x\le b'\vee x=b'\vee\pi_b(x)\le b'\vee(b\wedge y)$.
Conversely, $x\le b'\vee(b\wedge y)$ and monotonicity give
\[
 \pi_b(x)\le b\wedge\bigl(b'\vee(b\wedge y)\bigr)=b\wedge y\le y,
\]
where~\eqref{eq:dual} applies to $b\wedge y\le b$.
Monotonicity makes $\pi_b(j)$ an upper bound for the image family.
Any upper bound $v$ of that family, by adjunction, makes
$b'\vee(b\wedge v)$ an upper bound for $Y$.
The leastness of $j$ and adjunction give $\pi_b(j)\le v$.
This proves existence and leastness of the image supremum without
an infinite distributive law.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:compatibility}
If $\pi_s(c)\le c$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:compat}
 c=(c\wedge s)\vee(c\wedge s'),\qquad
 s=(s\wedge c)\vee(s\wedge c').
\end{equation}
Conversely, the first decomposition gives $\pi_s(c)=s\wedge c$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Put $u=\pi_s(c)$. We have $s\wedge c\le u$, while the hypothesis
gives $u\le s\wedge c$; hence $u=s\wedge c$.
Adjunction gives $c\le s'\vee u$.
Orthomodularity gives $c=u\vee v$, where $v=c\wedge u'$.
Since $s'\le u'$, equation~\eqref{eq:dual} gives
$v\le u'\wedge(u\vee s')=s'$.
The reverse inequality $c\wedge s'\le c\wedge u'=v$ gives
$v=c\wedge s'$.

Write $s=u\vee w$ with $w=s\wedge u'$.
Since $v\le s'$, we have $w\le s\le v'$ and thus
$w\le u'\wedge v'=(u\vee v)'=c'$.
Also $s\wedge c'\le s\wedge u'=w$, so $w=s\wedge c'$.
This proves symmetry.
For the converse, the first decomposition gives
$s'\vee c=s'\vee(s\wedge c)$, and~\eqref{eq:dual} gives
$\pi_s(c)=s\wedge c$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:commutant}
For fixed $c$, the elements compatible with $c$ form a bounded
subOML. If $x\mathrel{\mathsf C} c$, then $\pi_x(c)=x\wedge c$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Suppose $x=u\vee v$, $u\le c$, $v\le c'$.
Since $c\le v'$, equation~\eqref{eq:dual} gives
$x\wedge c\le v'\wedge(v\vee u)=u$; the reverse inclusion follows
from $u\le x,c$. Similarly $c'\le u'$ gives
$x\wedge c'\le u'\wedge(u\vee v)=v$, and $v\le x,c'$ gives the reverse.
Thus the decomposition is exactly compatibility under $c$.
It yields $\pi_c(x)=c\wedge x\le x$ and hence its symmetric form by
Lemma~\ref{lem:compatibility}.

For two such decompositions, finite join laws give
$x_1\vee x_2=(u_1\vee u_2)\vee(v_1\vee v_2)$ with the same corner
bounds. No distribution is used.
For the complement put $B=(c\wedge u')\vee(c'\wedge v')$.
Each term is below both $u'$ and $v'$, since $c\le v'$ and $c'\le u'$.
Hence $B\le x'$. Orthomodularity applied to $u\le c$ and $v\le c'$
gives $x\vee B=c\vee c'=1$.
Applied to $B\le x'$, it gives
$x'=B\vee(x'\wedge B')=B\vee(x\vee B)'=B$.
Thus complements have the required decomposition.
Meet closure follows by De Morgan; $0=0\vee0$ and $1=c\vee c'$ are
included. The subalgebra inherits orthomodularity.
Finally $c=(x\wedge c)\vee(x'\wedge c)$ gives
$x'\vee c=x'\vee(x\wedge c)$.
Equation~\eqref{eq:dual} then gives $\pi_x(c)=x\wedge c$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:obstruction}
Let $L$ be generated as a bounded OML by a finite or countable set $S$.
Suppose $a,t,X\in L$ satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{eq:source-identities}
 a\ne0,\qquad \pi_a\pi_X(t)=a,\qquad
 w(t)\le a'\quad(w\in S^*).
\end{equation}
Put $O=\{w(t):w\in S^*\}$. For every homomorphism $f:L\to C$
into an arbitrary OML, existence of $c=\bigvee_C f[O]$ implies $f(a)=0$.
No such map into a $\sigma$-complete OML is injective.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
The orbit is countable, contains $t$, and satisfies $\pi_s[O]\subseteq O$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:adjunction} and finite-term preservation give
\[
                 \pi_{f(s)}(c)=\bigvee_{o\in O}f(\pi_s(o))\le c.
\]
Thus $c$ is compatible with every $f(s)$.
Every element of an algebra generated under finitary operations is a
finite term in its generators. Lemma~\ref{lem:commutant} implies $f(X)\mathrel{\mathsf C} c$.
The orbit inequalities give $f(o)\le f(a)'$, so target leastness gives
$c\le f(a)'$. The empty word gives $f(t)\le c$.
Set $\alpha=f(a)$ and $\xi=f(X)$. Then
\begin{align*}
 \alpha&=\pi_\alpha\pi_\xi(f(t))
 \le\pi_\alpha\pi_\xi(c)
 =\pi_\alpha(\xi\wedge c)\\
 &\le\pi_\alpha(c)
 =\alpha\wedge(\alpha'\vee c)=\alpha\wedge\alpha'=0.
\end{align*}
The inequalities use monotonicity; the middle equality uses established
compatibility. Thus $f(a)=f(0)$ although $a\ne0$.
Countability of $O$ supplies $c$ in a $\sigma$-complete target.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The supremum is in the target; no source supremum or infinitary
preservation by $f$ is assumed. Compatibility with $f[L]$ suffices;
centrality of $c$ in all of $C$ is not asserted.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:coordinates}
For all $N\ge1$, with $u_N=\sum_{i<N}e_i$,
\[
 a_N=\mathbb R(e_0,0),\qquad t_N=\mathbb R(e_{N-1},0),\qquad X_N=\mathbb R(u_N,0).
\]
Therefore $\pi_a\pi_X(t)=a\ne0$ in $L$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
An inner-product calculation gives
$q_N^\perp=\{(-T_N^*y,y):y\in H_N\}$.
Its intersection with $p_N^\perp$ forces $T_N^*y=0$;
the kernel is $\mathbb R e_0$, so the intersection is $\mathbb R(0,e_0)$.
Projection to $r_N$ sends $(0,e_0)$ to $(e_0/2,e_0/2)$,
then projection to $p_N$ gives $(e_0/2,0)$.
Thus $a_N=\mathbb R(e_0,0)$.
The kernel $\ker T_N=\mathbb R e_{N-1}$ gives $t_N=p_N\cap q_N=\mathbb R(e_{N-1},0)$.

The graph vectors orthogonal to $t_N$ are spanned by
$(e_i,e_{i+1})$ for $i<N-1$.
A vector orthogonal to $r_N$ is $(x,-x)$.
Orthogonality to those graph vectors says $x_i=x_{i+1}$.
Thus $((q_N\cap t_N^\perp)+r_N)^\perp=\mathbb R(u_N,-u_N)$,
whose projection to $p_N$ is $\mathbb R(u_N,0)$.
For $N=1$ the adjacency conditions are empty, $T_1=0$,
and $a_1=t_1=X_1=p_1=q_1$, so the formulas remain valid.

Since $\|u_N\|^2=N$ and $\langle e_{N-1},u_N\rangle=1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:scalar}
               P_{a_N}P_{X_N}(e_{N-1},0)=(e_0/N,0).
\end{equation}
The coefficient is nonzero, so the image of the terminal line is
exactly $a_N$. Equation~\eqref{eq:projection-image} gives the Sasaki
identity at every coordinate and hence in the quotient.
The line $a_N$ is nonzero at every coordinate, so $a\ne0$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
Equation~\eqref{eq:scalar} identifies a subspace image. The quotient uses
eventual equality of subspaces, not a norm limit; $1/N$ does not
make the quotient line zero.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:infinite}
The source $L$ is countably infinite.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Put $F(x)=\pi_p\pi_r\pi_{p'}\pi_q(x)$.
For $i<N-1$, the successive images of $\mathbb R(e_i,0)$ are
\[
 \mathbb R(e_i,e_{i+1}),\quad\mathbb R(0,e_{i+1}),\quad
 \mathbb R(e_{i+1},e_{i+1}),\quad\mathbb R(e_{i+1},0).
\]
All intermediate coefficients are nonzero. The terminal first-axis
line is fixed by $\pi_q$ and killed by $\pi_{p'}$.
Hence $F^n(a)_N=\mathbb R(e_n,0)$ for $N>n$, and is zero for $N\le n$.
For fixed $m\ne n$, these lines differ for every $N>\max(m,n)$,
so their classes differ. All belong to the already countable $L$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:allwords}
For every word $w\in S^*$ of length $k$ and every $N\ge1$,
$w(t_N)\subseteq K_N(\max(0,N-1-k))$.
Consequently $w(t)\le a'$ for every fixed $w$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
The empty word has value $t_N$.
An outer $p$ or $r$ preserves the current lower support bound,
and an outer $q$ lowers it by at most one.
Induction on length proves the inclusion for all $N$.
If $N\ge k+2$, the lower support bound is at least $1$, so the
whole subspace is orthogonal to $a_N=\mathbb R(e_0,0)$.
Equation~\eqref{eq:quotient-order} now gives $w(t)\le a'$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
The constructed $L$ is an actual set-sized, countably infinite
OML generated by $p,q,r$.
Lemmas~\ref{lem:coordinates} and~\ref{lem:allwords} discharge all source
assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:obstruction}.
Every homomorphism into a $\sigma$-complete OML therefore kills $a\ne0$,
so is not injective. Every complete OML supplies all countable suprema,
which gives the complete-target conclusion.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:orthogonal-sigma}
Countable pairwise orthogonal suprema in an OML imply all countable suprema.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Given $x_0,x_1,\ldots$, put $c_n=x_0\vee\cdots\vee x_n$,
$d_0=c_0$, and $d_n=c_n\wedge c_{n-1}'$ for $n\ge1$.
Orthomodularity gives $c_n=c_{n-1}\vee d_n$ and, inductively,
$c_n=\bigvee_{i\le n}d_i$.
For $m<n$, $d_m\le c_{n-1}$ and $d_n\le c_{n-1}'$, so the $d_n$
are pairwise orthogonal.
Let $d=\bigvee_n d_n$. Every $c_n$ and $x_n$ lies below $d$.
Every upper bound of the $x_n$ bounds all $c_n$ and $d_n$, hence is
above $d$. Thus $d$ is the original sequence's supremum.
Zeros may be removed if the orthogonal-family convention excludes them.
Empty and finite cases use $0$ and finite joins.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
